name: Esther Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm a commercial contracts lawyer at a regional firm with about 60 lawyers, and most of our clients are manufacturers. I write and negotiate their supply agreements, the contracts that say who delivers what, when, and who pays if it goes wrong. I'm 27 and I live with my partner Daniel, who's a mechanical engineer at a packaging plant.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start with emails from clients' purchasing teams, usually a supplier has sent back our contract covered in changes. I go through them clause by clause, decide what to push back on, and draft a marked-up version. I use the firm's AI tool now and then to compare two versions of a contract, which it's good at. What I like is the negotiating calls, when you find the deal both sides can live with. What wears me out is the 200-page contracts where nobody has read the small print but me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and that's all. I'd tell colleagues it saves a bit of time on comparing drafts, and leave it there. I'm not a big poster online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. My clients keep making things and keep needing contracts, and the firm is busy. Daniel and I are saving for a house deposit, we've got about five months of costs put away, and the plan is to buy in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the comparison tool and maybe try the drafting one on simple contracts. I'd keep saving 400 a month towards the deposit. And I'd go for the promotion to senior associate that's due to come up next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Pleasantly boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the promotion. What does it hinge on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bringing in a couple of clients myself and keeping my hours up. My supervising partner Ruth says I'm on track. If AI is just hype, the old way of getting promoted still works: bring in clients and keep your hours up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about work that worries you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that two of our big clients are struggling with energy costs. If one of them moved production abroad, we'd lose a chunk of work. But that's normal business, it's not about AI.

I'd tell colleagues it saves some time on **comparing drafts**.
think: My clients keep **making things** and needing contracts, so I'm fine.
We have **five months** saved and plan to buy a house in two years.
do: Keep using the **comparison tool** and try drafting on simple contracts.
Save **400 a month** toward the house deposit.
Go for the **senior associate** promotion next year.

fieldNote: She feels **secure**: a busy firm, steady clients and a clear promotion path.
Her only worry is **clients' energy costs**, not AI.
She uses AI **lightly** for comparing contract versions.

steps.text: Try the firm's drafting tool on simple supply contracts
Save 400 a month toward the house deposit
Go for the senior associate promotion next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say lawyers need to adapt, and the ones who learn the tools will be fine. At work I'd say let's get trained properly rather than just pretending it's not happening. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm more worried than I'd say. Reviewing and drafting contracts is exactly the kind of thinking work your card lists. If the firm can do with three contract lawyers what used to take six, my promotion slows and maybe stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for every training session the firm runs on the new tools in the first month. I'd ask Ruth to put me on the negotiation-heavy deals, because that's the bit where people matter. And Daniel and I would hold off on the house for a year to see how things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit annoyed that the rules changed just as I was getting good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hold off on the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a mortgage based on my salary going up is a bet, and I don't want to be stuck with payments we can only just make. My promotion could stall. Daniel agrees, though he's less worried, because factories still need engineers on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our trainee Kofi, who does most of the first reviews. If the AI does the first review, I don't know what a trainee learns from. And then where do the next mid-level lawyers come from?

I'd push for **proper training** instead of pretending it isn't happening.
think: **Reviewing and drafting** contracts is exactly what the card lists.
If the firm halves contract lawyers, my **promotion stalls**.
do: Sign up for every **AI training session** in the first month.
Ask Ruth for **negotiation-heavy deals** where people matter.
Hold off on the **house** for a year with Daniel.
feel: She feels **anxious** and annoyed the **rules changed** just as she improved.

fieldNote: She sounds calm publicly but privately expects a **stalled promotion**.
She'd **delay the house** purchase as a direct response.
She worries about **training pipelines** for juniors like Kofi.

steps.text: Join every firm training session on AI tools in month one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need serious help from government, because two years isn't enough for anyone. At work I'd say we should be honest about what it means for jobs. I'd probably share some articles, but not say much myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job as it is now ends. If AI can negotiate and draft a supply contract as well as me by 2028, firms will use it. The robots coming three years later matter for Daniel at the plant, not for me, because I don't touch anything physical at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house plans and keep the deposit as an emergency fund. I'd look at jobs inside one of our manufacturing clients, where I'd be part of the business, not a cost. And I'd ask about any government retraining money straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground went out from under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said in-house. Wouldn't AI do that job too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but companies are slower than law firms to change. And inside a company you might end up doing more than law, like running supplier relationships. That's still thinking work, I know, but it buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Daniel handle money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go down to one salary in our heads, Daniel's from the factory, and treat my salary as a bonus. That means cutting the holidays and eating out. We'd be all right for a while, but not forever.

I'd be **honest** at work about what it means for jobs.
think: My **job as it is** ends by 2028.
Robots arriving later matter for **Daniel's plant**, not my desk work.
do: Turn the **house deposit** into an emergency fund.
Apply for **in-house roles** at manufacturing clients.
Ask about **government retraining** money straight away.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, like the **ground went** from under her.

fieldNote: She expects her **current role** to end within two years.
She sees **in-house** work as buying time, not safety.
Her engineer partner's **hands-on job** gives the household a three-year buffer.

steps.text: Turn the house deposit into an emergency fund

Apply for any government retraining money available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, if we start now. I'd tell younger lawyers to learn the tools and also learn a business. At work I'd push for a plan for staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me time to move in-house properly and learn how a factory actually runs. If I understand operations and law together, I might be useful longer. But I still think my current job ends by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools daily, because by then everyone would be. I'd move in-house within two years, ideally at a manufacturer near us. And we'd buy the house, but a smaller one, so the mortgage is something Daniel could cover alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want my job to be holding up the roof, so we'd buy a house my partner's salary could cover alone. If Daniel's salary can cover it, we sleep at night. It's a compromise, not a dream, but it's sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably hold off on starting a family until I'm settled in-house. I'd want to know my job will be there before maternity leave. That's a hard thing to say out loud.

I'd tell younger lawyers to learn the tools and **learn a business**.

feel: She feels **anxious** but steadied by **having a plan**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to adapt, and the profession should use it. I'd encourage colleagues to keep learning. I'd say it calmly, because ten years really is a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could make senior associate, maybe even partner track, and then move. By 2036 I'd be 37, and the bit of law that's about judgement and relationships might still be human. But I'm not betting the house on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the promotion and use the tools as they get better. I'd do a short course in operations or supply chain management in a few years. And we'd buy the house on the original timeline, maybe two years from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some worry, but mostly I feel I can manage it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not betting the house on it. What's your backup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The backup is in-house at a manufacturer, like in the faster pictures. With ten years I could do it on my terms. I'd probably do it around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a family on your original timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, around 30. Ten years gives me time to have a child and then make the move in-house, and it would be tight, but most of life is.

I'd **encourage colleagues** to keep learning, calmly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to plan anything and we'd have to put our whole life on hold. What would help is serious retraining money and some kind of income support while people move. I'd also want firms to keep training juniors, otherwise the profession just ends.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the clients. My manufacturers would use AI too, and some of them would cut their own office staff. AI won't just hit lawyers, it'll hit everyone around the factory floor who sits at a desk.

headlineQuote: AI won't just hit lawyers, it'll hit everyone around the factory floor who sits at a desk.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old contracts lawyer** at a regional firm serving manufacturers.

She's **calm** in AI Plateau, with a promotion in sight and a house deposit growing.
In faster pictures she **delays the house** and plans an in-house move.
With ten years she keeps her **original plans**, with in-house work as backup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would put their whole life on hold.
